steps.body:
If a curve starts and ends at the **same height**, it must have turned round somewhere.

**Rolle's theorem:** if f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one c inside where **f′(c) = 0**.

It sounds too obvious to be worth a name. It is the engine of everything in this chapter.

explanationVariants: f(0) = 0 and f(4) = 16 − 16 = 0, so Rolle applies. f′ = 2x − 4 = 0 gives c = 2.
The parabola goes down and comes back up; the vertex is where it turned.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x² − 4x on [0, 4]. Note f(0) = f(4) = 0. Find the c that Rolle guarantees.

commonErrors.feedback: That is an endpoint. Rolle promises a c strictly INSIDE the interval: f′ = 2x − 4 = 0 gives c = 2.
Also an endpoint. The flat tangent is at the vertex, x = 2.
That is the coefficient. Set f′ = 2x − 4 to zero: x = 2.

steps.body: Why the hypotheses are not decoration.

widget.prompt: Break each condition in turn, and watch the theorem fail.

panels.title: Drop differentiability
panels.body: Take f(x) = |x| − 1 on [−1, 1]. The ends match (both 0), it is continuous — and f′ is NEVER zero. The corner ate the flat spot. Differentiability is not a technicality.

panels.title: Drop continuity
panels.body: A function that jumps can start and end at the same height without ever turning round. Continuity is what forces it to come back the way it went.

panels.title: Drop f(a) = f(b)
panels.body: Then there is nothing to prove — a curve that ends higher than it started need never be flat anywhere. It can climb the whole way.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — each hypothesis is load-bearing.
widget.successFeedback: Every condition earns its place: |x| − 1 kills the theorem with a single corner.

explanationVariants: f(x) = |x| − 1 on [−1, 1] has f(−1) = f(1) = 0 and is continuous — but f′ is −1 or +1 everywhere and never 0. Differentiability fails at the corner.
The theorem does not merely fail to apply; its conclusion is genuinely false here.

widget.prompt: f(x) = |x| − 1 on [−1, 1] has f(−1) = f(1) = 0, yet f′ is never zero. Which hypothesis fails?

options.label: Differentiability — there is a corner at x = 0.
options.feedback: Right, and it is the whole point: without differentiability the curve can turn round at a corner, where there is no tangent to be flat.

options.label: Continuity.
options.feedback: |x| − 1 is perfectly continuous — you can draw it without lifting the pen. The failure is in the SLOPE, not the value.

options.label: f(a) = f(b).
options.feedback: Both ends are 0, so that hypothesis holds. Something else has broken.

options.label: None — Rolle is simply false.
options.feedback: Rolle is a theorem, and theorems do not fail. What fails is a hypothesis — differentiability, at the corner.

steps.body:
Rolle also counts your roots for you.

Between any two roots of f there must be a root of f′. So if f′ has only **two** zeros, f can have at most **three** roots — because four roots would force three flat spots.

The derivative constrains the function, which is the reverse of the usual traffic.

explanationVariants: Between consecutive roots of f, Rolle forces a root of f′. With only 2 roots of f′, there can be at most 3 roots of f — a fourth would demand a third flat spot.
It is a counting argument, and it is the first time the derivative has been used to constrain f rather than describe it.

widget.prompt: f′ has exactly 2 zeros. What is the MAXIMUM number of roots f can have?

commonErrors.feedback: Rolle gives a root of f′ BETWEEN each consecutive pair of roots of f. Three roots of f need only two gaps, so two zeros of f′ suffice.
Four roots of f would create three gaps, each demanding its own zero of f′. With only two available, four roots are impossible.
You can certainly do better than one — three roots are compatible with two zeros of f′.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 3 roots create 2 gaps, and 2 zeros of f′ can fill them. A 4th root would need a 3rd zero.

hints: First check the hypotheses: is f(0) = f(3)? Compute both.
f′ = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2), which is zero at x = 0 and x = 2. Which one is strictly INSIDE (0, 3)?
explanationVariants: f′ = 3x(x − 2) is zero at 0 and 2, but Rolle promises a c strictly inside (0, 3). Only c = 2 qualifies — x = 0 is an endpoint.
The theorem is careful about that: the flat spot is guaranteed in the OPEN interval.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 3x² on [0, 3]. Find the c strictly inside that Rolle guarantees.

commonErrors.feedback: f′(0) = 0 is true, but 0 is an ENDPOINT. Rolle promises a c strictly inside the open interval (0, 3), and that is c = 2.
f′(3) = 27 − 18 = 9, not zero — and it is an endpoint besides.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f′ = 3x(x − 2) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2; only x = 2 lies strictly inside (0, 3).

steps.body: Same height at both ends means a flat spot in between.
takeaways: Rolle: continuous, differentiable, f(a) = f(b) ⇒ some c inside has f′(c) = 0.
Every hypothesis is load-bearing — |x| − 1 breaks the conclusion with a single corner.
Between consecutive roots of f there is always a root of f′, which lets the derivative COUNT the function's roots.
steps.teaser: Next: tilt the picture, and Rolle becomes the Mean Value Theorem.

concept.body: If you leave home and come back to the same height, you must have stopped climbing at some point. That is the whole theorem — and the flat spot is guaranteed strictly BETWEEN the two ends, never at them.

explanationVariants: f′ = 2x − 6 = 0 gives c = 3, the vertex — and f(0) = f(6) = 0, so Rolle applies.
For a parabola the guaranteed c is always the vertex.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x² − 6x on [0, 6], where f(0) = f(6) = 0. Find c.

commonErrors.feedback: An endpoint. The flat tangent is strictly inside, at the vertex x = 3.
Also an endpoint. Set f′ = 2x − 6 to zero: x = 3.
